doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
title: Reissues, Frank Kofsky and musicians as businessmen
summary: Ware and Gloria talk about reissues, an article on who owns jazz, and how a musician cannot also run the business.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: But, even though they haven't re-issued it, we saw it a couple years ago in a record store on the lower East Side for twenty-some dollars, and it's not as old as some of the older ones that were reissued.

Yeah. Well, like Riverside of Japan is bringing out a whole lot of old Riverside records, you know, and well, it's big business. The conglomerates are doing it. I was reading this periodical call Black Perspectives and this guy, Frank Kofsky wrote ....

Yeah. He wrote an article in there called "The State of Jazz" and he is very informative about who owns what, and which way jazz, as I know it, is headed, came to be, and he is not a musician, but he can take time to check all those facts where, as a musician, it's hard for us to get to the material, you might say.

But we know what's going on, just like I was saying being a musician and coming off the bandstand, the club owner looked like he wanted to hide you somewhere -- when you're not in the club, go anywhere, just get out of my sight, you know.

But this is something that should have been dealt with by some other people, perhaps, and you can't expect a musician to create the music, to take care of the business, and do all that, even though people somehow expect that, I think it's too much to expect.
It is. Now you can't create nothing worrying about how many people come in the club and things like that.
Well, even like Duke Ellington, with his -- he had a fantastic business sense along with his music, but even he had to have other people to help him. He just couldn't do everything else himself.
